subtopic: Facing an ethical breach at work
subtype: Approach: leaving when the culture will not change [Revision]
passage:
Darshan had raised the concern three times: once in a team meeting, once in an email to the director, once in a quiet corner with the head of finance. Each time the answer was the same: "We'll look into it." Each time nothing changed.
On a Sunday evening in his Delhi flat, Darshan thought about the fourth time and realised it would not be a fourth attempt. It would be a decision to stay. "If I stay and say nothing, I'm part of it," he told himself.
He made a plan. He updated the CV, wrote to two former colleagues, and put a handover date on the calendar for after the current project. Then he met Vasudha, now at another firm, for coffee to ask what her workplace was really like.

qa.q: How many times had Darshan raised the concern?
qa.a: Darshan had raised it three times.

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling on Sunday evening?
qa.a: Darshan felt frustrated and resigned, and was clear that staying silent would make him part of it.

qa.q: What could Darshan do while working out the notice period?
qa.a: Darshan could keep doing the work honestly, keep dated notes of the concerns raised, and prepare a clean handover.

qa.q: How might Vasudha see Darshan's questions about her workplace?
qa.a: Vasudha probably saw someone serious about finding values that match, and may have felt honoured to be asked for an honest picture.

grounding: The passage shows an employee whose repeated concerns are ignored, deciding that staying would mean joining the practice and starting a planned search for a workplace that fits.

subtopic: Facing an ethical breach at work
subtype: Approach: leaving when the culture will not change [Revision]
passage:
'I'm starting to look for another job,' Anirban said, putting down his fork.
Anjali looked up. 'Because of the billing thing?'
'Because of the third time. I raised it in March. Then in June with compliance. They sent a note saying "noted". Yesterday my manager asked me to sign off on the same kind of invoice.'
'Did you sign?'
'No. But if I stay, one day I'll be the one who signs. That's how it works there.'
'We have the flat EMI.'
'I know. I'm not resigning tomorrow. I'll apply quietly, ask in interviews how they handle complaints, and leave only when I have an offer.'
Anjali was quiet, then pushed the rice bowl toward him. 'Make a list of companies. I'll ask my cousin about hers.'

qa.q: When did Anirban raise the issue with compliance?
What is Anirban afraid of if he stays?
qa.a: He is uneasy that one day he will give in and become the person who signs such invoices.

qa.q: What could Anirban ask in interviews, and why?
qa.a: He could ask how the company handles complaints or ethics concerns, so he doesn't move to a place with the same culture.

qa.q: How does the plan look to Anjali?
qa.a: Anjali is worried about the flat EMI at first, but the careful plan lets her back it and even offer help.

grounding: It shows an employee whose repeated concerns are ignored deciding that staying would mean joining the practice, and starting a planned search for a better-matched workplace.

subtopic: Facing an ethical breach at work
subtype: Approach: leaving when the culture will not change [Revision]
passage:
I'm Leela, and I left the agency last month after two years there. People ask if it was the pay. It wasn't.
Three times I raised the same thing: we were writing claims for a health drink that the lab report didn't support. The first time, my creative head said, 'Clients expect a little stretch.' The second time, I wrote to HR. Nothing. The third time, I sat in a meeting and heard myself defending a line I knew was false. That scared me more than any boss.
So I made a plan. I updated my portfolio at night, asked Farhan, who had left the year before, how his new firm handled client pressure, and applied only to places that answered that question honestly. When the offer came, I resigned politely and handed over my files in order.

qa.q: How many times did Leela raise the issue?
What scared Leela most, and why?
qa.a: Leela was frightened to hear Leela's own voice defending a false line, a sign that the culture was changing Leela too.

qa.q: What else could Leela look for in the next workplace?
qa.a: Leela could ask future colleagues, not only interviewers, how client pressure is handled, to check that the answer is real.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel being asked about his new firm?
qa.a: Farhan may feel glad to help someone facing what he once did, and understand why the question mattered.

grounding: It shows an employee leaving after repeated ignored concerns, deciding that staying would mean joining the practice, and searching for a workplace with matching values.
